title: Digestion & Absorption (Extended)
description: Starch digestion by amylase and maltase, pepsin and trypsin in contrasting pH conditions, bile in emulsification and neutralisation, and absorption through villi, capillaries and lacteals for Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610 Supplement.

notes.heading: From Starch to Glucose: Amylase Then Maltase (7.4.6)
notes.body:
📌 The two-stage Supplement pathway
**starch → maltose → glucose**
• **Amylase** catalyses **starch → maltose**. Pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion in the small intestine.
• **Maltase** catalyses **maltose → glucose**. Maltase is located in the **epithelium of the small intestine**, so the final step occurs at the absorbing surface rather than only in the intestinal lumen.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Name the enzyme, substrate and product separately. Amylase does NOT complete starch digestion to glucose: it produces maltose. Maltase then hydrolyses maltose to glucose, the small soluble sugar that can be absorbed.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'amylase → glucose', or placing maltase in the stomach. Learn the pair as **amylase makes maltose; maltase makes glucose**, with maltase on the small-intestine epithelium.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Amylase: starch → maltose.
• Maltase: maltose → glucose at the small-intestine epithelium.

notes.heading: Pepsin and Trypsin: Same Reaction Type, Different pH (7.4.7)
notes.body:
📌 Two named proteases
• **Pepsin** acts in the **stomach**, where hydrochloric acid provides an **acidic** optimum pH.
• **Trypsin** acts in the **small intestine**, where conditions are **alkaline**.
Both contribute to the chemical digestion of protein, which is completed to small soluble amino acids for absorption.

🔑 Why location matters
An enzyme's optimum pH matches its normal working environment. Pepsin is adapted to acidic gastric juice; trypsin is adapted to the alkaline small intestine. Moving an enzyme away from its optimum changes the shape and fit of its active site and reduces its activity.

💡 Worked Example
Enzyme P digests protein fastest at pH 2, while enzyme T is fastest at pH 8. Identify P as **pepsin** and T as **trypsin**: use the pH optimum AND the site of action, not simply the word 'protease'.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying that pepsin needs alkaline conditions or that trypsin works in the stomach. The correct pairs are **pepsin–acid–stomach** and **trypsin–alkali–small intestine**.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Both are proteases, but their pH optima and sites differ.
• Low activity away from the optimum results from altered active-site shape and fit.

notes.heading: Bile: Emulsification and Neutralisation (7.3.7, 7.4.8)
notes.body:
📌 Two distinct functions
Bile is made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the duodenum.
1. **Emulsification:** bile breaks large fat droplets into much smaller droplets. This increases the total surface area of fat available to lipase, so fat digestion is faster.
2. **Neutralisation:** alkaline bile helps neutralise acidic food arriving from the stomach, providing suitable alkaline conditions for enzymes such as trypsin in the small intestine.

🔑 Physical preparation, not chemical digestion
Emulsification changes droplet SIZE, not fat molecules into new products. Lipase must then catalyse **fats and oils → fatty acids and glycerol**. Bile is **not an enzyme**: it has no active site and does not catalyse this hydrolysis.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that bile 'digests fat'. Award-winning wording is: **bile emulsifies fat, increasing surface area for lipase action**. Add neutralisation only when the question concerns stomach acid or intestinal pH.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Bile = emulsifier + acid neutraliser, not an enzyme.
• Smaller droplets mean greater surface area and faster lipase action.

notes.heading: Integrated Digestion in the Duodenum
notes.body:
🔑 Connect the processes in a logical sequence
Acidic food leaving the stomach contains partially digested starch and protein together with large fat droplets. In the duodenum:
1. **Bile helps neutralise the acid**, shifting conditions towards the alkaline optimum of intestinal enzymes.
2. **Bile emulsifies fat**, producing many small droplets with a much larger total surface area.
3. Pancreatic **amylase** continues **starch → maltose**, **trypsin** continues protein digestion, and **lipase** catalyses **fat → fatty acids + glycerol**.
4. **Maltase on the epithelial membranes** completes **maltose → glucose** at the surface where absorption occurs.

💡 Worked Example
If bile flow is blocked but pancreatic enzymes are still released, predict TWO effects: fat digestion slows because emulsification and surface area decrease, and the small intestine becomes more acidic because neutralisation is reduced. Do NOT predict that lipase itself has been removed.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Treating each secretion as an isolated fact. Extended questions often require a causal chain: secretion → physical or pH change → effect on enzyme activity → change in products formed.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Bile prepares the conditions and the fat surface; enzymes catalyse the chemical breakdown.
• Maltase provides the final starch-to-glucose step at the epithelium.

notes.heading: Villi and Microvilli: A Large, Thin Absorbing Surface (7.5.3–7.5.4)
notes.body:
📌 Structures to identify
A **villus** is a finger-like projection of the small-intestine wall. Its outer **epithelium is one cell thick**, giving a short distance between digested food in the lumen and the transport vessels in the villus core.
**Microvilli** are tiny projections of the epithelial-cell membranes. Villi multiply the absorbing area of the intestine, and microvilli increase that area still further.

🔑 How structure speeds absorption
• Many villi and microvilli → **very large surface area**.
• Thin epithelium → **short diffusion distance**.
• Dense capillary network → absorbed molecules are carried away, helping maintain concentration gradients.
• A central lacteal provides a separate route for fat digestion products.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing the two levels of folding: villi are projections of the intestinal wall; microvilli are much smaller projections on individual epithelial cells. Neither is a blood vessel.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Large area + short distance + transport away = efficient absorption.
• Identify epithelium, microvilli, capillary network and lacteal on diagrams.

illustration.alt: Labelled villus showing microvilli on a one-cell-thick epithelium, a blood capillary network and a central lacteal, with separate absorption routes for glucose and amino acids into blood and fatty acids and glycerol into lymph.
illustration.caption: Villi and microvilli increase surface area; the thin epithelium shortens the absorption path. Capillaries and the lacteal carry different digestion products away.

notes.heading: Capillaries Versus Lacteals: Two Absorption Routes (7.5.5)
notes.body:
📌 Blood capillary route
**Glucose and amino acids** cross the epithelium and enter the **blood capillaries** of the villus. Blood flow transports them away, preventing their accumulation and helping maintain diffusion gradients from the intestine into the blood.

📌 Lacteal route
**Fatty acids and glycerol** are absorbed into the **lacteal**, a lymphatic vessel in the centre of the villus. Lacteals drain into the lymphatic system; they are not blood capillaries.

🔑 Read diagrams by structure and contents
The capillaries form a branching network around a central, blind-ended lacteal. If asked for the destination of a nutrient, first identify the nutrient class: carbohydrate and protein digestion products take the blood route; fat digestion products take the lymphatic route.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that ALL nutrients enter the blood directly from a villus, or that glucose enters a lacteal. Keep the two routes separate.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Glucose + amino acids → capillaries → blood.
• Fatty acids + glycerol → lacteal → lymph.

notes.heading: Extended Applications: pH, Rates and Villus Diagrams
notes.body:
💡 pH and rate data
Compare like with like: same enzyme, substrate concentration and temperature. The enzyme with high protein-digestion activity at low pH is pepsin; the one favoured at alkaline pH is trypsin. A lower activity is shown by a SLOWER rate or a LONGER time for the substrate to disappear — do not reverse these.

💡 Bile experiments
With lipase, substrate, temperature and pH controlled, adding bile should increase the initial rate of fat digestion because emulsification increases surface area. Bile WITHOUT lipase can make droplets smaller but cannot produce fatty acids and glycerol by chemical digestion.

💡 Diagram and prediction questions
On a villus, trace each route from lumen → epithelium → vessel. Use the central vessel for fat digestion products and the surrounding network for glucose and amino acids. If villi are damaged or microvilli are lost, predict reduced surface area and therefore slower absorption, rather than a complete loss of enzyme secretion.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Explaining every result only with 'more enzymes'. In these applications the changing factor may be pH, droplet surface area, absorbing surface area, or the transport route.

✅ Check
Can you explain one pH result, one bile result and one villus-damage result as a complete cause-and-effect chain?

flashcards.definition: Catalyses the breakdown of starch to maltose; pancreatic amylase acts in the small intestine.
flashcards.example: Amylase produces maltose, not glucose directly.

flashcards.definition: An enzyme on the membranes of the small-intestine epithelium that catalyses maltose → glucose.
flashcards.example: Maltase completes starch digestion at the absorbing surface.

flashcards.definition: A protease that acts in the acidic conditions of the stomach.
flashcards.example: Pepsin has high protein-digesting activity at about pH 2.

flashcards.definition: A protease that acts in the alkaline conditions of the small intestine.
flashcards.example: Trypsin is favoured by the neutralised conditions of the duodenum.

flashcards.definition: The breakdown of large fat droplets into smaller droplets by bile, increasing surface area for lipase.
flashcards.example: One large oil droplet becomes many tiny droplets without changing fat into fatty acids.

flashcards.definition: Alkaline bile helps neutralise acidic food from the stomach, creating suitable conditions for intestinal enzymes.
flashcards.example: Neutralisation in the duodenum favours trypsin activity.

flashcards.term: Why bile is not an enzyme
flashcards.definition: Bile does not catalyse chemical digestion and has no active site; it emulsifies fat and helps neutralise acid.
flashcards.example: Bile alone cannot hydrolyse fat into fatty acids and glycerol.

flashcards.definition: Finger-like projections of the small-intestine wall that greatly increase the surface area for absorption.
flashcards.example: Many villi provide a much larger absorbing surface than a flat intestinal wall.

flashcards.definition: Tiny projections of epithelial-cell membranes that increase the absorbing surface area of a villus still further.
flashcards.example: Microvilli are much smaller than the villus on whose epithelial cells they sit.

flashcards.definition: The one-cell-thick outer layer of a villus, giving a short diffusion distance for absorbed nutrients.
flashcards.example: Glucose crosses this thin layer before entering a blood capillary.

flashcards.definition: Blood vessels that absorb glucose and amino acids and transport them away, helping maintain concentration gradients.
flashcards.example: After protein digestion, amino acids enter the capillaries rather than the lacteal.

flashcards.definition: A central lymphatic vessel in a villus that absorbs fatty acids and glycerol.
flashcards.example: Fat digestion products enter the lacteal and are transported in lymph.

questions.stem: Which product is formed when amylase acts on starch?
choices: Glucose
Maltose
Amino acids
Fatty acids and glycerol
questions.explanation: Amylase catalyses starch → maltose. Maltase then catalyses maltose → glucose at the small-intestine epithelium; the other products come from protein and fat digestion.

choices: In the acidic fluid of the stomach
Inside large fat droplets in the duodenum
On the surface of blood capillaries
In the epithelium of the small intestine
questions.explanation: Maltase is located on the membranes of the small-intestine epithelium, where it converts maltose to glucose at the absorbing surface. It is not a stomach enzyme or a component of capillaries.

choices: It is a protease acting in acidic conditions in the stomach
It is a protease acting in alkaline conditions in the small intestine
It is a carbohydrase acting on the membranes of the small-intestine epithelium
It is an emulsifier released into the duodenum
questions.explanation: Pepsin is the stomach protease and is adapted to the acidic environment provided by hydrochloric acid. Trypsin is the protease acting in alkaline small-intestine conditions.

questions.stem: A protease functions best in alkaline conditions in the small intestine. Which enzyme is it?
choices: Pepsin
Maltase
Trypsin
Lipase
questions.explanation: Trypsin is the named protease acting in alkaline small-intestine conditions. Pepsin acts in the acidic stomach; maltase digests maltose, and lipase digests fats rather than protein.

questions.stem: Bile is added to a mixture of oil and water, but no lipase is present. What happens?
choices: The oil is chemically digested to fatty acids and glycerol
Large oil droplets become smaller droplets, but the fat molecules are not chemically digested
The oil is converted directly into glucose
The oil droplets join to form one larger droplet with less surface area
questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies oil into smaller droplets, a physical change that increases surface area. Without lipase, fat cannot be enzymatically hydrolysed to fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.stem: Acidic food enters the duodenum from the stomach. Which function of bile directly helps trypsin work effectively?
choices: Converting protein into amino acids
Breaking fat into smaller droplets
Destroying pepsin molecules
Neutralising acid to provide more alkaline conditions
questions.explanation: Alkaline bile helps neutralise the incoming acid, moving the duodenum towards the alkaline conditions in which trypsin works best. Emulsification aids lipase, not trypsin directly.

questions.stem: How do microvilli improve absorption by the small intestine?
choices: They increase the surface area of the epithelial cells
They secrete additional lipase into the lumen
They pump blood through the capillary network
They neutralise stomach acid
questions.explanation: Microvilli are tiny projections of epithelial-cell membranes and greatly increase absorbing surface area. They are not glands, pumps or alkaline secretions.

questions.stem: Which pair of absorption routes is correct?
choices: Glucose → lacteal; amino acids → capillaries
Fatty acids and glycerol → capillaries; glucose → lacteal
Glucose and amino acids → capillaries; fatty acids and glycerol → lacteal
All digested nutrients → lacteal
questions.explanation: Glucose and amino acids enter the blood capillary network. Fatty acids and glycerol enter the central lacteal for transport in the lymphatic system.

questions.stem: On a villus diagram, label X points to the one-cell-thick outer layer whose cells bear microvilli. What is X?
choices: The lacteal
The epithelium
The capillary network
The intestinal lumen
questions.explanation: The epithelium is the villus's one-cell-thick absorbing layer, and its cells carry microvilli. The capillaries and lacteal lie inside the villus core.

questions.stem: Equal protein samples are digested under two pH conditions. Enzyme P takes 6 minutes at pH 2 and 55 minutes at pH 8; enzyme T takes 50 minutes at pH 2 and 5 minutes at pH 8. Which identification is correct?
choices: P is trypsin and T is pepsin
P is maltase and T is amylase
P and T are both lipase
P is pepsin and T is trypsin
questions.explanation: A shorter time means faster digestion. P works fastest in acid, so it is pepsin; T works fastest in alkali, so it is trypsin. Their contrasting pH optima match stomach and small-intestine conditions.

questions.stem: Four tubes contain equal fat samples at the same temperature and pH. Times for complete fat digestion are: A lipase + bile, 4 min; B lipase alone, 13 min; C bile alone, no digestion; D neither, no digestion. What best explains these results?
choices: Bile increases fat surface area for lipase but cannot chemically digest fat without lipase
Bile digests fat faster than lipase but only when lipase is present
Lipase works by neutralising bile
Bile converts lipase into trypsin
questions.explanation: Lipase plus bile is fastest because emulsification creates more fat surface area for lipase action. Bile alone gives no digestion because it is not an enzyme and cannot hydrolyse fat.

questions.stem: A person's small-intestine epithelium lacks functional maltase, but pancreatic amylase is normal. Which outcome is most likely after starch enters the small intestine?
choices: No maltose can be formed from starch
Starch is converted directly into fatty acids
Maltose can still form, but much less glucose is produced from it
Trypsin replaces maltase and produces glucose normally
questions.explanation: Normal amylase can still produce maltose from starch. Without maltase, the next step — maltose → glucose — is greatly reduced; trypsin is a protease and cannot digest carbohydrate.

questions.stem: The bile duct becomes blocked, while pancreatic enzyme secretion continues normally. Which prediction is best?
choices: Starch digestion stops because amylase cannot be released
Fat digestion slows and neutralisation of stomach acid in the duodenum is reduced
Protein digestion stops because trypsin is no longer produced
Glucose absorption increases because more lacteals form
questions.explanation: Less bile means less emulsification, so lipase has a smaller fat surface area and digestion slows. Reduced alkaline bile also reduces neutralisation; pancreatic enzyme production is unaffected.

questions.stem: A disease damages many villi and microvilli, but digestive enzyme secretion remains normal. What is the most likely direct consequence?
choices: Faster absorption because nutrients travel a shorter distance
No chemical digestion anywhere in the intestine
Slower absorption because the absorbing surface area is reduced
More fat absorption because every lacteal enlarges
questions.explanation: Villi and microvilli provide the large absorbing surface. Their loss reduces surface area and absorption rate even though enzymes can continue to digest food normally.

questions.stem: Which sequence best integrates digestion in the duodenum?
choices: Bile helps neutralise acid and emulsifies fat → pancreatic enzymes continue chemical digestion → epithelial maltase converts maltose to glucose
Pepsin emulsifies fat → bile converts maltose to glucose → trypsin neutralises acid
Maltase neutralises acid → lipase digests protein → glucose enters a lacteal
Bile chemically digests fat → amylase produces amino acids → fatty acids enter blood capillaries
questions.explanation: Bile adjusts pH and increases fat surface area; pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase then continue chemical digestion, and epithelial maltase completes maltose → glucose. The other options swap enzymes, substrates and routes.
